detail.title: Calculate Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and Specificity Using a Confusion Matrix
detail.description: Using carseats_train and carseats_test, fit a decision tree predicting sales_cat with max depth 1, min n 2 and seed 1234, build the test confusion matrix and compute (1) accuracy, (2) precision, (3) recall, (4) specificity; (5) interpret with STAR. Round to two decimals.
detail.understand: The model is trained on the 319 training stores and judged on the 81 unseen test stores (model validation, §8.4). 'min n' (tidymodels) corresponds to sklearn's min_samples_split. The positive class must be stated: here 'High' (as in Table 8.3 and the book's script, where High is coded 0 and placed first).

questions.prompt: Compute the accuracy on the test data.
Compute the precision on the test data.
Compute the recall on the test data.
Compute the specificity on the test data.
Interpret the confusion matrix using the STAR Framework.

detail.interpretation: A single split on shelf location gives moderate accuracy, good precision and specificity, but low recall for High stores.
common_mistakes: Using `sales` as a feature (it reveals sales_cat — leakage).
Mixing up matrix layouts: Table 8.3 has predicted in rows, sklearn's confusion_matrix has actual in rows.
Using the book's printed specificity formula TN/(TN+FN).
detail.python_code:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

train, test = pd.read_csv("carseats_train.csv"), pd.read_csv("carseats_test.csv")
X_train, y_train = train.drop(columns=["sales", "sales_cat"]), train["sales_cat"]
X_test,  y_test  = test.drop(columns=["sales", "sales_cat"]),  test["sales_cat"]

encode = ColumnTransformer([("dummify", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False),
                             ["shelf_location", "urban", "us"])], remainder="passthrough")
model = Pipeline([("prep", encode),
                  ("tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, min_samples_split=2, random_state=1234))])
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, model.predict(X_test), labels=["High", "Low"])  # rows = actual
TP, FN, FP, TN = cm[0, 0], cm[0, 1], cm[1, 0], cm[1, 1]
print("accuracy   ", round((TP + TN) / cm.sum(), 2))
print("precision  ", round(TP / (TP + FP), 2))
print("recall     ", round(TP / (TP + FN), 2))
print("specificity", round(TN / (TN + FP), 2))
notes: Uses the book's official carseats_train.csv (319 stores) and carseats_test.csv (81 stores) from github.com/datasci4all/Datasets.
DS4A p.383 prints specificity = TN/(TN+FN); the standard definition, used here and in the book's Python script, is TN/(TN+FP).

answers.explanation: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) = 43 / (43 + 5) = 43/48. (DS4A p.383 prints TN/(TN+FN) = 0.67; that formula is the negative predictive value. The book's own Python script computes TN/(TN+FP).)

answer.Scope: Car-seat sales at 319 training and 81 test stores; response sales_cat (High > 8,000 units, Low otherwise); 10 explanatory variables (sales excluded because it determines sales_cat).
answer.Track: How well does a one-question tree predict High-selling stores in new (test) stores, and which errors does it make? Positive class = High.
answer.Articulate: The tree uses one split: shelf_location is not Good → predict Low; shelf_location is Good → predict High. On the 81 test stores it is right 55 times (accuracy 0.68). When it says High it is usually right (precision 0.71), but it finds only 12 of the 33 truly High stores (recall 0.36); it correctly labels 43 of 48 Low stores (specificity 0.90).
answer.Respond: Many High stores are missed (false negatives). If missing High stores is costly, grow a deeper tree or add variables (e.g. price) and compare recall on the test data.
